stops.name: Sunlight
stops.heading: Sunlight is a stream of photons
stops.body: The Sun sends out light of many wavelengths at once, and together they look white. A prism bends each wavelength by a different amount, so white light fans out into colours. Light comes in tiny packets called photons. The shorter the wave, the more energy each photon carries.
stops.try: Slide to pick a photon. Its colour, wavelength and energy change together.
stops.alt: A glowing Sun on the left shines a white beam into a glass prism. A fan of colours comes out the other side, violet bent the most and red the least, and lands on a screen. One photon, drawn as a short wave, travels along the colour you picked. Below, a chart shows how much sunlight reaches the ground at each wavelength, with the visible part coloured in.
stops.chart: Sunlight at the ground, by wavelength (ASTM G173 standard spectrum). The coloured band is the part you can see.
stops.note: The prism angles are worked out for real flint glass. The fan is drawn 3 times wider so you can see it.

stops.name: The leaf
stops.heading: Why leaves look green
stops.body: Chlorophyll, the pigment in leaves, is very good at catching red and blue light and poor at catching green. Photons that are not caught can bounce back out of the leaf and into your eye. More of those are green, so the leaf looks green.
stops.try: Send one photon of your colour, or watch the rain. Whether it is caught is decided by real measured chlorophyll spectra.
stops.alt: Coloured photons rain onto a large green leaf. Red and blue ones mostly vanish into the leaf with a small flash: they were caught. Green and yellow ones more often bounce back up toward you. Counters show how many were caught and bounced, and a colour patch shows the mix of light bouncing back, which comes out green. The chart shows how strongly chlorophyll a and b absorb each wavelength.
stops.chart: How strongly chlorophyll a and b absorb each wavelength (measured in a liquid called ether, not in a leaf). The shaded curve is the chance a photon is caught.
stops.note: The chance uses chlorophyll a and b in the mix found in the leaf's light-harvesting complex: 24 a to 18 b. Carotenoids, which also catch blue light, are left out. A real leaf scatters light around inside, so it catches more green than this, and green light gets deepest into the leaf.

stops.name: Into the cell
stops.heading: Into the leaf, into a cell

levels.name: Leaf layers
levels.body: A leaf is many cells thick. Light passes the clear top layer and reaches tall cells packed with green chloroplasts.
levels.alt: A cut through a leaf: a clear top layer of flat cells, then a row of tall cells full of green beads, then looser round cells. The photon streaks down into one of the tall cells.

levels.name: Plant cell
levels.body: Plant cells, like all cells with a nucleus, are about 10 to 100 micrometres across. Each one has a cell wall and many chloroplasts, the parts that do photosynthesis.
levels.alt: One plant cell with a box-like wall, a big clear vacuole in the middle and green chloroplasts lined up around the edge. The photon heads for one chloroplast.

levels.name: Chloroplast
levels.body: A chloroplast has an outer and an inner membrane. Inside are stacks of flat discs called thylakoids. A stack is a granum, and the fluid around the stacks is the stroma.
levels.alt: Inside a chloroplast: a see-through double skin and many green stacks of coin-like discs joined by thin sheets, floating in pale fluid. The photon dives toward one stack.

levels.name: Thylakoids
levels.body: Chlorophyll sits in the thylakoid membrane, held in place by proteins. This is where the photon is finally caught.
levels.alt: Close to a stack of thylakoid discs. The membrane surface is dotted with protein bumps that hold chlorophyll. The photon is about to hit one of them.

stops.try: Zoom in step by step, or press Play.
stops.note: Inside the cell, sizes are drawn to fit the screen, not to scale.

stops.name: The antenna
stops.heading: Caught, passed on, put to work
stops.body: One chlorophyll in a light-harvesting complex catches the photon. The energy then jumps from pigment to pigment without any light being given off. This is called resonance energy transfer, and it works best between pigments that are close together. At the reaction centre, called P680, the energy knocks out an electron. Water is split to replace it, and oxygen is released.
stops.try: Press Play to follow the energy. Drag to turn the complex.
stops.alt: A real light-harvesting complex: three protein chains drawn as soft ribbons hold 42 chlorophylls and 12 orange carotenoids, with a glowing magnesium atom at the centre of each chlorophyll. A flash marks where the photon is caught, then a glowing spark hops from chlorophyll to chlorophyll, with the distance of each hop shown. It leaves the complex for a drawn reaction centre, where an electron shoots out and two water molecules split, letting one oxygen molecule float away.
stops.caption: Real structure: pea light-harvesting complex II, PDB 2BHW. 42 chlorophylls (24 a, 18 b) and 12 carotenoids. Each magnesium atom glows.
stops.note: The atoms are real, from PDB 2BHW. This app picks the hop route using the real distances; in a leaf the energy spreads along many routes at once and reaches the reaction centre in about a millionth of a second. The reaction centre, electron and water are drawn as an illustration.

stops.name: What next
stops.heading: One photon, one step toward food
stops.body: That energy now drives the rest of photosynthesis. The plant uses it to make ATP and NADPH, then builds sugar from carbon dioxide in the stroma.
stops.alt: The leaf again, calm in the sunlight, with small bubbles of oxygen rising from it. Links lead to the rest of the explorer.

facts.t: A photon's energy is E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f the frequency. Since f = c / λ, E = hc / λ.
Planck's constant h = 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J/Hz, the speed of light c = 299 792 458 m/s and the elementary charge e = 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, all exact (CODATA 2022). 1 eV = e × 1 volt.
Visible light is the narrow part of the spectrum between about 400 nm and about 750 nm that the human eye responds to.
Shorter wavelengths carry more energy than longer ones.

In glass the index of refraction is greatest for violet light, so a prism bends violet more than red. The prism uses the flint glass values in OpenStax Table 1.2 (1.662 at 660 nm up to 1.698 at 410 nm) with Snell's law and a 60° prism.

The sunlight curve is the ASTM G173-03 global tilt reference spectrum: sunlight at the ground through 1.5 air masses onto a surface tilted 37°. The photon rain samples photons in proportion to this curve.

Colours on screen are worked out from the CIE 1931 colour matching functions and converted to screen colour with the W3C sRGB formulas. Pure single wavelengths are more vivid than any screen can show, so these are the nearest screen colours.
Chlorophyll a absorbs blue and red but not green. Because green is reflected or transmitted, chlorophyll looks green. Carotenoids absorb in the short-wavelength blue region.
The chlorophyll curves are measured spectra in diethyl ether from the PhotochemCAD database: chlorophyll a peaks near 428 and 660 nm, chlorophyll b near 453 and 643 nm.
The chance of being caught is an illustration built from those spectra: chlorophyll a and b mixed 24 to 18 as in the LHC-II trimer, given a thickness that catches 95% at the strongest peak.
Green light reaches deeper into a leaf than red or blue light, and leaves use chlorophylls that absorb green weakly.
Eukaryotic cells, which include plant cells, have diameters of 10 to 100 μm. Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole.
Inside the chloroplast are stacked disc-shaped thylakoids with chlorophyll in their membrane. A stack is a granum; the fluid around it is the stroma.
The pea LHC-II trimer holds 42 chlorophylls a and b, 12 carotenoids and 6 lipids (2.5 Å X-ray structure, PDB 2BHW).
Each LHC-II monomer has 8 chlorophyll a and 6 chlorophyll b, with all the chlorophyll b around the borders between monomers.

A light-harvesting complex has many antenna pigments, 300 to 400 chlorophylls in all for each photosystem, and passes energy from chlorophyll to chlorophyll to the reaction centre in about a millionth of a second. Only energy moves, not electrons.
Resonance (Förster) energy transfer passes energy from an excited pigment to a neighbour without giving off light. Its efficiency falls with the sixth power of the distance.
Plants tune how they catch light to the light around them, and protect themselves from too much light.
Chlorophyll b's red peak (643 nm) is a shorter wavelength than chlorophyll a's (660 nm), so its excited state holds a little more energy. That is why energy tends to flow from b to a.

P680 is the reaction centre of photosystem II. Its lost electron is replaced from water; splitting one water molecule gives two electrons, two hydrogens and one oxygen atom, so two are split to make one O₂.

vocab.definition: A tiny packet of light. Every photon moves at the speed of light and carries a set amount of energy, E = hf.
The distance from one crest of a wave to the next. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy than longer ones.
The narrow band of light, from about 400 to about 750 nanometres, that the human eye can see.
A tiny unit of energy that suits single photons. It is the energy one electron picks up crossing 1 volt, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ joules.
The green pigments that catch light for photosynthesis. They absorb blue and red light well but not green, which is why leaves look green.
Yellow, orange or red pigments that also sit in the thylakoid membrane. They catch blue light and safely get rid of extra energy as heat.
The part of a plant cell that does photosynthesis. It has an outer and an inner membrane around stacks of thylakoids.
A flat, disc-shaped sac inside a chloroplast. Chlorophyll and the photosystems sit in its membrane, so this is where light is caught.
A stack of thylakoids, like a pile of coins. More than one are called grana.
The fluid around the thylakoid stacks inside a chloroplast. This is where the plant uses the energy from light to make sugar from carbon dioxide.
Proteins holding many chlorophylls and carotenoids that work like an antenna. They catch photons and pass the energy on to the reaction centre.
How energy jumps from an excited pigment to a nearby one without giving off any light. It gets much weaker as the pigments move apart.
The heart of a photosystem. A special pair of chlorophyll a molecules there turns light energy into an excited electron.
One of two light-catching machines in the thylakoid membrane, made of a light-harvesting complex and a reaction centre. Its reaction centre, P680, takes electrons from water and releases oxygen.
